title: Gluttony and temperance
hook: too much, too fast, too fussy

segments.voice: Yesterday, greed and generosity: the manna that went bad overnight. Your line was open hands. What did you give that you hadn't planned to? Day one thousand two hundred six.

Esau comes in from the field, starving. His brother Jacob has a pot of red lentil stew on the fire. Esau doesn't even name the dish. In the King James words he says, "Feed me, I pray thee, with that same red pottage; for I am faint." Jacob names a price: your birthright, the eldest son's inheritance. And Esau, in the moment, can only see the bowl. He swears, he eats, he drinks, he gets up and goes. The text ends it with one flat line: "thus Esau despised his birthright." A whole future, for one meal, right now. Today: gluttony and temperance.

Gluttony sounds like a sin about eating too much, and that's part of it. But some Christian teachers saw more than size in it. Gregory the Great, a pope and teacher, listed the ways a person can go wrong at the table, and only one of them is quantity. Eating too soon, before the time. Eating too lavishly, always needing the expensive thing. Eating too much. Eating too eagerly, wolfing it down. And eating too fussily, where it all has to be prepared just so. Too much, too fast, too fussy. Each one, in a different way, makes the food the center of the world. That's what happened to Esau. Hunger is not a sin; he really was faint. But in that moment the bowl got bigger than everything else, bigger than his family, his future, his promise. The letter to the Hebrews remembers him exactly that way, as the one "who for one morsel of meat sold his birthright." One morsel. So what's the opposite? Christian tradition calls it temperance, and it isn't joyless. When Jesus fed the crowd on the hillside, the Gospel slows down before anyone eats: he took the loaves and the fishes, and "looking up to heaven, he blessed, and brake." A look up, a blessing, and then the bread. The answer to gluttony isn't eating less food so much as receiving food differently. Paul widens it: "whether therefore ye eat, or drink, or whatsoever ye do, do all to the glory of God." That's one reason some Christians begin a meal with a pause, a grace. Some say a set prayer, some a few words of their own, some only bow their heads for a breath. That pause puts the bowl back in its place: a gift, not a master.

Here's the practice: eat one meal slowly. You can start now, even without food. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind the next meal you'll eat today. Where will you be? What will be on the plate? Before it comes, decide on a small pause at the start. A breath, a few words of thanks, a glance at who grew it, cooked it, carried it. If you pray, you can say a grace you already know. Then picture taking the first few bites slowly enough to taste them. The bell holds the time.
Gluttony and temperance. Letting food become the center, too much, too fast or too fussy; and receiving it as a good gift, with thanks.
Your line: eat with thanks. Today, choose one meal, pause before the first bite, and eat it slowly enough to taste it. Day one thousand two hundred six.

howItsDone: Some Christians say grace before meals, some with a set prayer and some in their own words, and some churches keep fasting days; Christian teaching on the deadly sins pairs gluttony with temperance.

original.note: Latin: the throat, and the old Latin name for the deadly sin of gluttony.

trapdoor: what you thought: gluttony means overeating.
what it means: letting food become the center: too soon, too much, too eagerly, too lavishly, too fussily. its opposite receives food with thanks.
what a scholar hears: Gregory the Great's ways of sinning at the table, later taken up by Thomas Aquinas.

notes: Gregory the Great's list (Moralia 30.18; taken up by Aquinas, ST II-II q.148 a.4: praepropere, laute, nimis, ardenter, studiose) is paraphrased as too soon, too lavishly, too much, too eagerly, too fussily. No count is spoken. Confirm the renderings.
'Some Christian teachers saw more than size in it' rests on Gregory and Aquinas; confirm.
'some Christians begin a meal with a pause, a grace'; confirm.
Hook: 'red lentil stew' combines Genesis 25:30 (red pottage) and 25:34 (pottage of lentiles). Confirm.
Practice avoids writing a new prayer; it invites 'a grace you already know'. Avoids repeating day 1200 (temperance: stop one thing at enough).

Editor pass: fixed the garbled 'That.s'; cut the invented detail of the smell filling the tent (Genesis 25:29 says only that Jacob sod pottage); 'Esau doesn't even name the dish' follows 25:30 ('that same red'); howItsDone 'many Christians' softened to 'some'.

Audit (2026-10-02): 1 Timothy 4:4 ('every creature of God is good... received with thanksgiving') was quoted here in the teach and myth and also on day 1200 (temperance) in its teach and myth; replaced with Matthew 14:19 (Jesus blesses before feeding the crowd). Gregory's 'studiose' now glossed 'prepared just so' (food too elaborately prepared) rather than 'nothing is ever quite right'.
